I will be permanently taken off off of it. 
I hope this helps . Am I a freak of nature?  Thanks for letting me share. I feel no one is listening.

author: @EatLoveLaugh79
text: Since everyone's sharing their experiences, I would like to share mines too. I've been on Ozempic for 6 months now. I've been one of the fortunate ones to not have any side effects. I didn't lose my cravings until my dose went up 1.0 mg. Though I'm not curbing my appetite, I am gradually losing my weight a total of 30 lbs now...that means approx 5 lbs a mth and a little over 1 lb a week.  I think that is really good because I'm not losing so drastically all at once and more at a healthy weight.  My A1C went from a 7.0 to a 5.3 after 5 mths.  I couldn't be happier since I am Type II Diabetic and only needed to do this once a week.  It really beats injecting myself with insulin twice a day, every day, when I had Gestational Diabetes.  I was scared at first that my insurance wouldn't cover it this year since the doctor said that all insurances now are re-evaluating their coverage with these type of medicines.  However, after my prior authorization was approved, I haven't had a standstill with my refills.  Last year's insurance sucked.  I paid almost $600 after insurance and a secondary $150 off discount card for my first pen.  Other pens after that was $74.  Switched insurances this year and I'm now only paying $24.99 a pen. I'm very happy with everything now:  my health, my weight, and the costs.

What doesn’t make sense to me or at least people aren’t being really transparent about is using it by those who aren’t diabetic… who don’t have other, underlying health conditions stating they use it for weight loss because nothing else, like diet, lifestyle and activity levels didn’t work.

Unless I’m misunderstanding, the main mechanism / action of these meds in non-diabetic, otherwise healthy adults is by reducing appetite.

Don’t take my comment as me being judgmental towards anyone using this medication. If it helps people be healthier in the long run, go for it.

My issue comes in the form of supply and demand. I think there should be a tier level to identify those who NEED it versus those who WANT it. At least while there’s a shortage.

I also find myself mentally side-eyeing pharmaceutical manufacturers. I have no hesitation in expressing these companies are in no huge rush to fill inventory. While there’s a mass wave of demand, their profits go through the roof.

text: I'm diabetic and obese at 59 yo. I lost 60 lbs in 2024 on Mounjaro (280 to 220 lbs) after my weight had previously plateaued at 280 after a previous net weight loss of 40 lbs (what I kept off from the previous 4 years before 2024 on keto diet alone). I was referred by my new doctor to an endocrinologist diabetic/weight loss program that employed Mounjaro (after my employer discontinued Kaiser Permanente, which never told me about this option - KP is unwilling to insure it; seemingly, the doctors must be discouraged to advise it). If there are risks with these drugs (although Ozempic and Mounjaro are not in the same chemical class of drug), there are greater risks with diabetes and obesity. I couple Mounjaro use with a Keto diet and intermittent fasting. With any weight-loss program, there's always an alarm about "muscle loss," but much of what is happening is one is losing fluids and inflammation in one's muscles, not muscle tissue itself (making muscular folks appear to have shrinking muscle, but the pure muscle mass is not being consumed by the weight loss). The body turns to its fat reserves so long as insulin (weight gaining hormone) is kept low, and leptin (weight loss hormone) is allowed to elevate, as when one is in ketosis. I have also been reversing my diabetes completely. I'm at the level of prediabetes now (A1C from 11.0 in June 2024 to 5.8 in December 2024). This saved my life and from future miseries of diabetic afflictions in old age. I also read that even putting aside exercise, a great cause of many diseases is a lack of sunlight and abundant fresh oxygen. So, I have also undertaken to take my dog on long daily walks (giving us both exercise) and breathing in the fresh air (oxygen is an enemy to cancers) and robustly increasing my vitamin D with sunlight exposure. I experience no side effects from Mounjaro. I now take 10 mL once a week (having moved up from 2.5, 5.0, and 7.5 mL). I stay at my current dose as long as it still feels effective in suppressing my appetite, especially at night - my worse time to overeat. My mind is also given time to reconsider overeating, as when I'm feeling full, yet some tape in my mind tells me I want to eat - as for comfort or to curb anxiety/stress. I then focus on the fact that I'm not even really hungry, and I can ignore those old mind tapes. I also find myself forced to rethink my portion controls, especially on occasions where I order takeout (which is much less these days), but when I do order takeout, I find that my old beliefs of the portions that I need to satisfy me turn out to be too much food. I have to throw food away. My mind still needs to reprogram these "takeout" tapes in my head -- my eyes (and memory) are truly bigger than my stomach these days. My endocrinologist tells me that Mounjaro is even good for sleep apnea, which makes sense if one is losing weight, less constriction in one's neck. My older brother recently lost a lot of weight after gastro-bypass surgery. I have now passed him. They say that these drugs will replace the old surgeries. Big limitations to the drug may result if you continue a diet that has sugars, fructose, and high carbs. Regardless of the quantity, these foods spike insulin levels (the weight gain hormone), which makes weight loss impossible during these times - even more impossible if one is nibbling small meals all throughout the day - the old, bad "6 meal/day" myth. A ketogenic diet (even carnivore leaning) is the most compatible diet in my experience.

author: @SilentSpecter4u
text:
Stop lying Oprah. Modern Western Black women face unique challenges when it comes to prioritizing their health and well-being, often falling behind women of other backgrounds in this regard. Too frequently, a lack of personal accountability and awareness, coupled with societal pressures, leads some to embrace an attitude that demands acceptance without self-improvement, particularly when it comes to physical health. 

While many invest heavily in external appearances, spending hundreds or thousands on wigs, weaves, cosmetic procedures, or chasing a fast-paced, curated lifestyle, the focus on genuine health, like maintaining a healthy weight or sustainable self-care, often takes a backseat.

Life is fleeting, and it’s critical to recognize its brevity. Instead of leaning on excuses or expecting unconditional acceptance, Black women can empower themselves by starting today, investing in their health with the same energy they dedicate to their outward image. 

The expectation of grace without discipline creates a double standard, especially when some are quick to critique Black men while overlooking their own inconsistencies. True growth comes from structure and commitment, not fleeting trends or superficial relationships that lack depth or mutual respect.

The reality is, health and self-respect are universal standards, not unique to any one group. Black women, like anyone, deserve relationships built on mutual effort and accountability, not fleeting connections rooted in low standards. By prioritizing inner strength and discipline, Black women can redefine their narrative, fostering healthier lives and relationships that reflect their true worth.

author: @bruceangel4459
text:
Very few people want to age prematurely and die any earlier than is absolutely necessary. I’ve found if they have the information and it’s a reasonable ask, they’ll do it, has been my experience.

The power of daily brisk walking for the mathematical benefits is a reasonable ask, the benefits are many and the attributes are easy to see and prove.

It works. 

Prove it to yourselves.

Think about how much or how little you actually walk. If you’re like most people you walk from your home to your car and from your car to your destination and this is exactly *not* how it is supposed to be.

If you practice the power of daily brisk walking for the mathematical benefits it will change your physicality, your countenance, your mind and then quite possibly your life. 

If you stick with the power of daily brisk walking for the mathematical benefits you will have more energy, you’ll feel more mentally secure and at some point you might even begin to feel as if you’re aging in reverse. 

This is the power of daily brisk walking for the mathematical benefits.

I know it probably sounds unbelievable but the good news is that you can easily prove or disprove it to yourself. 

Here’s how:

(Cue pre-written text)

This is quite possibly the best information that you’re going to receive in this lifetime. I call it the power of daily brisk walking for the mathematical benefits. And if it does what I say it will do, you will share it with your family, friends and loved ones until the end of time or the end of your family line, whichever comes first.

We humans were meant to walk every day and to feel, look and be our optimal best we have to walk briskly everyday. 

*Practicing the art of daily brisk walking for the mathematical benefits will change your physicality, your countenance, your mind and then quite possibly your life.*

When this works for you, share it with your parents/family, friends and loved ones if you want to catch a glimmer of what they were like when they were young because the power of daily brisk walking will age them in reverse.

The power of daily brisk walking works fast and efficiently and you can easily prove it to yourself.

Here’s how:

Take a selfie before you begin this process, then walk briskly everyday for the mathematical benefits that’ll payoff like compounding interest. 

After some time has passed, take another selfie. The difference should be easily discernible and readily apparent in your changing physicality and happier countenance. If you stick with it you’re going to look sharper, feel sharper and actually be sharper than you’ve been in some time. You’re going to look, feel and be happier and more energized than you’ve felt in a long time.

(No dieting or weightlifting is required)

When you walk: 

Open your eyes slightly wider and walk at a brisk pace, making sure to swing both of your arms while using your eyes for things both near and far & having as much fun as possible.

(It’s an eye exercise and brain training stimulator) 

At some point you’re going to feel as if your eyesight is improving and you’re aging in reverse. 

Google “brisk walking and telomeres”, lengthening your telomeres will have you feeling as if you’re aging in reverse. You’re going to feel healthier, happier, sharper and stronger than you have in quite some time if you just stick with it.

That’s it, it really is that simple.

We humans were meant to feel alive, healthy, happy, vibrant and vital all of our lives as we age. If you practice the art of daily brisk walking for the mathematical benefits you will experience all of these things. And unlike other activities this one, barring illness or injury is sustainable for the rest of your life.

Why does this work more efficiently and effectively than almost anything else at helping you achieve your goals?

Because we were designed/evolved and adapted over millions of years to do this one thing extremely well. Animals in the wild walk from shortly after birth until death in a never ending search for food and water or to escape predators. We humans eschew walking and ride in air conditioned comfort to air conditioned food stores and air conditioned gyms to walk slowly, workout a bit and stand around. 

It’s only been since the last hundred plus years and the invention of the automobile that we’ve forgotten that we’re supposed to walk and walk briskly everyday and the invention of the cellphone has only exacerbated the issue.

If we want to look, feel and be our optimal best we have to thoroughly mix the chemicals in our brains and bodies everyday. We have to walk and we have to walk briskly.

If you’re unaccustomed to walking briskly, fear not, just take it slow, your large muscles will adapt quickly and you have the rest of your life.

The leading cause of injury in adults is unintentional falls. 

*Practicing the art of daily brisk walking will improve your balance, mobility, agility and coordination making falls less likely.*

This is sustainable for the rest of your life and a guaranteed mood booster. 

Extras:

Make an AC/DC greatest hits playlist, push play and try to keep up. 

(This is a great brisk pace)

*Get psyched* *Get hyped* *Get fired up*

Eventually you’ll be able to recall this feeling easily and at will.

Dress lightly or you’ll overheat, feel sick and quit. 

I wear baselayer, synthetic in warm weather and wool in cooler weather. No jacket is required until approximately 10 degrees. 

Good, comfortable shoes or boots are a must.

When you walk seven days a week for years you’re going to experience every kind of weather. Something I’ve learned is that we humans have an amazing capacity to heat ourselves up quickly when we’re on the move and the rain, snow and cold will have little effect. Think about our caveman ancestors in skins, no underwear & no jackets and boy are we lucky and you’ll be warm and toasty. If you’re cold, just walk faster!

(You’ll be amazed at how quickly you’ll adapt if you just stick with it)

You’re going to sweat a lot, so stay well hydrated and drink water before you get thirsty.

Get an Apple Watch and close your rings daily, it’s cheaper than any trainer or gym and it will keep you disciplined and on track.

Good luck to you and remember to:

Open your eyes slightly wider and use them for looking at things both near and far while swinging both of your arms. *Remember to think happy thoughts when you walk and have as much fun as possible to achieve the maximum benefits.*

PS- This is everything that I’ve learned in eight years, distilled down to its essence and put in a nutshell to make it as easy as possible for you with the best possible outcome. This works, prove it to yourself by aging in reverse, remember to walk briskly everyday for the mathematical benefits.

PSS- Start slow and take it easy, you have the rest of your life to perfect the art of daily brisk walking. As always, check with a medical professional before beginning any program of exercise.

text:
I never had a weight issue at all, and never even needed to consciously watch my wieght until I hadmy first kid. Then, I suddenly gained over 100lbs and no specialist doctor was able to tell me why! With my next kid, I gained even more weight while on a strict 1200 calorie a day, low-carb diet. Never have been able to get ANY answers from doctors on why I couldn't lose weight despite trying the numerous diet & exercise plans they gave me. The best answer they could give was that it's some kind of metabolic/endocrine issue, but no doctor has ever had any answers more solid than that. 
Finally, I got sick of it (and thinking of my family history of type 2 diabetes was scary!) and asked my doctor for ozempic. Suddenly, for the first time in almost 18 years, I'm losing weight and steadily heading back to a healthy weight. Literally NOTHING else I've tried since having kids has ever resulted in me losing more than 1-2lbs. I finally feel like I'm getting back to something that feels even a bit more like "my" body, and it's amazing. I wouldn't judge anyone for taking these drugs, especially since they may have medical issues like me!

author: @justpassingthrough7437
text: Diagnosed with type 2 diabetes last November.  They treated me with good old fashioned insulin in the hospital. The endocrinologist I followed up with talked me into going on Ozempic even though I was already on insulin.  One pen gives you six once-per-week dosages.  I took the first dose and the painful cramps started immediately.  I forced myself to stay on it. By the third week (dose 3) I noticed my bowel movements were coming out like a paste.  It was a total literal mess! By week four, I was having one bowel movement every 2 weeks or so. My stress from the never-ending gut-punch pain and lack of bowel movements triggered my stress eating habits. I forced myself to finish the pen because I knew that there were thousands of other people out there who would give anything to get  a pen. I have exceptional insurance so the pens cost me nothing. I knew I was 'privileged' to have a pen. By the time I took that last dosage, IF I had a bowel movement I had to press down on my stomach with brute force to get my body to expel the waste. When it came out it was like squeezing toothpaste out of a tube. It spread all over no matter how far apart I spread my cheeks and how deliberately I positioned myself to try to get it out in the cleanest way. On top of that, the urge to go was sudden and immediate which means there was no 'holding it' until I got home like I usually could do.  So many times I used up an entire roll of toilet paper and wasted 8-10 flushes just to try to clean myself up enough to return to work and not be terrified that I would smell. I started using wet wipes against the policy clearly noted all over the restroom prohibiting the flushing of wet wipes in the company restroom.  I had no choice! I needed a full-on shower after every bowel movement. I would go 2-3 weeks without one but then the need (not urge - NEED) to go would hit me so hard and fast I had no choice but to go wherever I was.  Once I pulled over in a wooded area and went into a large styrofoam fast food cup. Needless to say my plans were canceled and I went back home because I don't keep toilet paper in my car. I was blessed I had that cup and it was just big enough. The stomach cramps were excruciating and remained whether I had had a recent bowel movement or not...  I never refilled my prescription.  I take the good old fashioned insulin and I am working really hard on the head and heart issues that are causing me to be so undisciplined with food.  If I fix my food I will fix the diabetes. If I fix my food I will fix my weight. Six months after my first doze of Ozempic I finally started to feel relief from the pain. I now have a bowel movement about once a week and about 2 weeks ago (now 9 full months since I stopped taking Ozempic) I had the first solid bowel movement I've had since January. No paste, just poop! I literally looked up at the ceiling and thanked God! A couple of weeks ago was also when I finally started having 3-5 bowel movements per week.  The need to go is still sudden, but at least it's solid and not a paste that spreads all over my nether regions against my will and despite all my efforts.  I really want to get back to the body I had until I was 30, but I'll just have to do it the old way.  I will never touch Ozempic again.  I have a brand new pen, still in the sealed box, in my fridge. It will stay there until.... My endocrinologist has since prescribed Monjauro and got my insurance to cover it. Every single time I consider filling that prescription I think of what the last 10 months have been like and I just cannot do it! I'm still waiting for all of the cramping to finally go away. Those whose experience with these drugs is symptom free, complication free and pain free are the winners here.

Diabétique type 2 et en surpoids , mon endocrinologue m'a prescrit ozempic. J'ai ressenti vraiment une propagande de la part de mon medecin . J'ai donc demarré 0.25mg , ensuite 0.5mg avec qui j'ai des troubles digestifs, urinaires , les nausées me coupe la faim et cela me force a adapter mon alimentation a sa plus simple expression et les effets disparaissent. Ces phénomènes s'attenuent à 3 jours de l'injection et recidivent . Je vais tenir en tout 7mois . Je n'ai plus de diabète, j'ai perdu 24kg , je suis epuisé , je ne digère plus rien .J'en informe mon endocrinologue qui me repond que c'est le prix a payer. Une douleur insupportable sur le ventre et dans le dos s'installe , je consulte mon medecin , il me prescrit une prise de sang avec les marqueurs du pancréas (lipase, amilase) et ils s'avèrent 8 fois de la norme maxi. author: @TheodoraKimmelHello
text:
I almost tried ozempic. I had gained a ton of weight, fifty pounds, from geodon, and was pre-diabetic. According to the BMI, I was 25 pounds overweight, and I was miserable having to eat cake almost everyday because of the geodon messing with my brain chemistry and making it impossible to concentrate. Coupled with that, I had childhood traumas surrounding eating making consuming food the only soothing act I was taught, and something that my parents had given me attention about consistently, regularly, and predictably.

I decided to go without it because I didn’t think it was the most appropriate for me. I have very slowly lost 25 pounds in 8 months using low calorie dieting, high protein and high fiber with low fat and sugar macros, and one hour of moderate exercise nearly everyday. I avoid alcohol as well.


I ended up doing what was right for me, and now know how to eat and eat well, enjoy being physical, and slowly losing weight in a manner that’s sustainable. It’s also annoying because the results aren’t huge the way you see on the internet, but they are right.

I learned how sleep impacts water retention, and how I have a lot of underdeveloped muscles. I don’t think Ozempic really helps with this, so although this has been hard, I learned a lot about my body that maybe the drug might have occluded.


It seems like ozempic is well suited for people who already don’t enjoy eating, but overeat due to compulsion, stress, and genetics. They just have big, almost senseless appetites where they want to eat healthy, but it’s like the wiring is frayed.


I did read some stories about what people did on ozempic and changed my dietary habits some to match them as if I was on ozempic.


The biggest difference has been consuming enough protein. I shoot for 1 pound of my weight to 1 gram of protein, and rely on mostly white meat chicken and nonfat milk based proteins. I have plans to eventually have vegan, high protein days 2-3 times a week, and ensure max is included in my diet, plus protein2O. I also have keto bread for the protein and fiber, but still eat complex carbs like rice and oats, and well as bevita crackers. I never consumer sugary sodas, but chocolate does belong in my diet in small amounts, especially during my period. Ice cream is the first choice for dessert, not cake or cookies, because ice cream soothes the nerves. Cake is I associate with parties, but it still is included every so often because it’s fun.

Ozempic might have helped, but I think people can do what I did. My friend tried ozempic and gained weight because his eating wasn’t due to appetite but due to depression.

author: @victoryvictorious633
text:
As someone who's been on a yo-yo diet all my life... only making long-term habits you can keep forever can keep the weight off.
 I've begun just slowly adding habits i can live with forever into my schedule now.
 I've begun weight lifting and just use exercises that i dont mind. Like i hate doing squats, it makes me avoid working out, so i find another exercise i dont mind like bulgarian split squats and hip thrusts instead. I hate most ab exercises except ab roller and ab pulldown, so now i only do those.
 Like this i can keep going forever, by figuring out what makes me avoid something and then just finding another way to do it. It doesn't have to be optimal to work.

With food, i just write out a list of food categories that are recommended by government dietary guidelines like dark leafy greens, meat/meat-substitutes(incl. Mushrooms, eggs), fiber-rich vegetables, legumes, etc. Then i choose min. 1 from each category to mix together to make a healthy meal. I use small plates to control portion size, and i write down when i eat (not what i eat) in a journal to keep an eye on my eating frequency.
 Experimenting with healthy tasty sauces and cuisines has been a game changer for eating more vegetables. Garlic yogurt is such a healthy and tasty salad sauce.
 The same with experimenting with fruit desserts (with very little or no added sugar) from a list of fruits, nuts, seeds and additions (eg. Yoghurt etc.).
Trying new healthy recipes is key. If you dont like the food and desserts you are eating, you won't be able to continue forever.

text: I was offered ozempic by my doctor, due to my weight and very strong family history of type 2 and gestational diabetes. I immediately declined. 1. I can’t stand needles. 2. Appetite suppression is the one thing the everybody is aware of when thinking of weight loss caused by Methylphenidate, but it also increases your metabolic rate as well. So instead of what everybody would be thinking… that I’m just starving myself… let me reassure you. I have one healthy full meal each day, and I also go on a 3km walk daily too. Combine that with the increased metabolic rate, gives you a bit more of a reassuring answer to my big success so far. And the fact that I have the energy and strength to go on that daily 3km without getting tired just proves that I’m not malnourished from the appetite suppression and abusing my medication. My mother was a CRNP in endocrinology (specializing in treating diabetes) and a former certified diabetes educator before that. Semiglutide is doing so much good and I love to see how many people are more able to enjoy life since they've been on it!

If you're eligible and a good candidate for semiglutide please ask your doctor about it! Also be aware that you can still have a negative response to taking this stuff.
Pro tip: antacids make the nausea manageable, but will delay stimulant absorption in the body. Neurodivergent people can and should bring this up with their doctors (if for no other reason than my PCP and my Psychiatric NP didn't tell me)

I don't know how things would have turned out if I didn't have help from this medication. If someone has to take medication to lose weight, why are they shamed? author: @kurgleplex
text:
Dec 7 2024, I was in a hospital bed, 300 pounds and bright yellow from a gall bladder that decided to clock out early. Bilirubin had backed into my Pancreas. I asked the surgeon about the scar tissue in my abdomen impacting the surgery, he told me "You are missing the point. You need to lose weight, or you are going to die. And you had better do it soon." He turned around and just walked out of the office, post-op visit, right in front of my wife. Some of you would be angry for sure, being talked to this way. I found it embarrassing, honest, and completely motivational.

And it worked. I know all the cliches are true, but hearing a surgeon who possibly just saved my life, frustrated after having to move a 100 lb slab of just raw fat out of the way so he could operate on somebody who, statistically, is probably not going to listen to a word he said. I could just tell I was wasting his time, and we both knew it. I had more sympathy for him then me, in a weird way. Anyway - 

Got on Mounjaro, dropped 70 pounds doing nothing but typing, I mean c'mon guys. Once I hit 220, I started running again, and almost a full year later from the gall bladder kerfuffle I am at 188.2, headed smoothly towards my rather arbitrary goal of 175, comfortably running 5K a day and moving persistently towards my first race. Oh, I'm 49. My life has meaning right now. I will never go back to what I was, I would rather die, plain and simple, and face it everyone, that is what is happening when you carry an extra hundred on you. Uncomfortable and true.

In my opinion, Terzapetide is a lifechanging solution for Diabetics who struggle with their weight. The real victory is when you drop enough weight and are then able to find a sustainable, enjoyable activity to commit to - Then turn that into your vehicle for change. Find your mountain, whatever it's called, and conquer it! I wish all of you success on your journey - You may not know it, but you are the best friend you will ever have. And I guarantee you owe yourself a favor by now.

got on mounjaro, dropped 70 pounds doing nothing but typing, i mean c'mon guys. once i hit 220, i started running again, and almost a full year later from the gall bladder kerfuffle i am at 188.2, headed smoothly towards my rather arbitrary goal of 175, comfortably running 5k a day and moving persistently towards my first race. oh, i'm 49. my life has meaning right now. i will never go back to what i was, i would rather die, plain and simple, and face it everyone, that is what is happening when you carry an extra hundred on you. uncomfortable and true.

in my opinion, terzapetide is a lifechanging solution for diabetics who struggle with their weight. the real victory is when you drop enough weight and are then able to find a sustainable, enjoyable activity to commit to - then turn that into your vehicle for change. find your mountain, whatever it's called, and conquer it! i wish all of you success on your journey - you may not know it, but you are the best friend you will ever have. and i guarantee you owe yourself a favor by now.

GLP-1 meds have been a very positive game changer for me. I have been on a roller coaster— losing weight and then gaining it back all my life. As I have gotten older, the ‘losing’ part became increasingly more challenging. Simply changing diet and exercise stopped working like they did when I was younger.  

My success with GLP-1’s—both in losing weight and keeping it off—has convinced me that putting the burden on people predisposed to obesity, suggesting that they just need to change their behaviour or try a little harder, is problematic.  Obesity is a disease in the same sense as cancer or heart disease. Changing behaviour is part of the equation for preventing these diseases, but sometimes even people who did everything ‘right’ will still need angioplasty or chemotherapy.

author: @0ckwordly
text:
I've been taking Zepbound (and several other medications) for about a year for Dercum's Disease. I had a really rough few months where I threw up constantly and had to go on medication to stop the vomiting and stomach issues, and even with it, I'd still feel sick. My body eventually adjusted, but I do still occasionally throw up and feel nauseous, especially the day after my shot day, and around medication times. I truck on despite not really needing to lose any more weight because the reduction in inflammation in my damaged adipose tissue from my disease has been significant enough that throwing up is better than being immobilized by pain and swelling. I've lost about 100lbs from GLP1s, and another 50 from a previous doctor-prescribed weight loss medication. Zepbound drastically changed my relationship with food and the types of foods I crave. The control on overall food intake helped me get used to cutting my sugar intake to improve my overall health with Dercum's (which, while unrelated to diabetes which i do not have, also worsens from sugar intake). For me, I've gained a lot and suffered a lot from the medication. I wouldn't recommend it for healthy people without excessive body fat, especially if exercise is a viable option for you. Dercum's Disease is worsened by movement of any kind, so I'm not supposed to move around a whole lot. GLP1s helped me maintain a caloric deficit in a rotating weekly schedule. I eat less in the days following shot day, and more towards the end of the week, and ive consistently lost 2-3 lbs a week while staying away from serious exercise, which is better for my individual case. 

EDIT: To comment on muscle loss, I definitely experience weakness. My disease causes general weakness, but I would not doubt that I have also lost muscle mass in my arms, as they feel particularly much weaker. My legs feel stronger than my arms, but heavier people tend to start out with a lot of leg muscle mass from carrying themselves around all day. So my previous hulk legs are probably just normal now. But i do get spuratic moments of leg weakness which comes on suddenly.

Leaving this here for anyone who may be reading wondering if this medication would be good for them.

I was prescribed Mounjaro for type 2 diabetes, yes it dropped my A1C and I lost over a hundred pounds...BUT the side effects kicked in about a year and a half later. I developed what's called Gastropresis, saliva started to regurgitate up into my mouth. Started to have smaller and smaller stools during bowel movements. Then eventually, complete constipation and extreme pains in my abdomen. Then I couldn't eat at all...any portion of food would make me want to vomit. I was scared to eat and these symptoms continued for months even after I stop taking the medication. Simply put, this drug shuts your stomach down. After months of going to the ER, PCP, and my Endocrinologist I finally went to a Gastrologist and prescribed numerous medications to get my stomach to function again (somewhat). My body was affected so badly by this drug that I had stomach issues for months afterwards, the last side effect was extreme acid reflux. It took approx a year or longer to fully get past of the major side effects and the muscle loss is a whole other issue I dealt and the feeling that your body was shutting down. I had NO energy NO strength anymore and just looked forward to night to come so I could just sleep and not be awake to experience all these symptoms for weeks and weeks. 
Its been a year since all of this has pass and I'm back to eating like a normal human again, I got my strength back gained about 65% of my weight back and A1C is high again but, I would rather take Metformin and Farxiga to deal with the diabetes. The phycological effects it had on me nearly broke me mentally. I will NEVER recommend anyone taking these TO GLP drugs for diabetes or weight loss!
The video talks about the benefits and side effects of this drug but not really mention the condition of gastropresis. Think before you take this...it was no guarantee that my body would recover after I stopped taking the Mounjaro. I would rather be fat and deal with high A1C than go back on this vile drug!

author: @madst82
text: I am on Mounjaro.  I have PCOS.  When I lost weight to get pregnant, I had to eat a diet of about 1000 calories/day, and exercise (cardio) at least 2 hours/day, 6 days a week, to lose weight.  It was legitimately so difficult to lose weight.  I was on Metformin to help, but it really did nothing for me without a severely restricted diet and an extreme amount of exercise.  I ultimately was lucky and got pregnant naturally. Once I had my daughter, there was no way that I could eat that diet while breastfeeding, and who had time or energy (I slept when she slept) to exercise that amount of time.  I gained most of the weight back that I lost to get pregnant.  And it stuck.  As I grew closer and closer to diabetes, I was prescribed Ozempic, but at a clinic that included a dietitian visit, a nutritionist visit, exercise consultation, and a gym. It was covered by insurance for the most part, but was still expensive.  But . . . it worked. I went from 203 to 165, and I'm sticking there.  My endo switched me to Mounjaro, but I figure where I'm at is all the medication can do for me, and the rest is up to me.  However, to get over the insane roadblock that PCOS puts in front of you (or me, at least) it was worth it because my kid is 14 and I'd like to be here for her as long as possible.  I did have side effects at first but overall, it has been a positive experience.  My husband also paid to use it because he struggled with alcohol abuse.  It completely shuts off the cravings for alcohol, but the medication is not FDA-approved for that and insurance does not cover it.  Again, it is worth the price to be around for our kid.   Ultimately, these medications give you the push and support your body needs to "get going" and "get motivated" to see results that you want to keep and to make lifestyle changes to maintain the good changes.  If you can afford it and stand the side effects, it is a scientific godsend for some individuals.

Flash forward to now and I am literally half the man I use to be. I weigh 165 pounds and feel fantastic. 

I can tell when the end of the week comes and it's time to take another shot. I get hungry and I call my last day my cheat day.  Ill treat myself with some ice cream or something sweet.  

It's been a long road, but because of my genetics, I don't think I would have been able to keep the weight off without the help of it.

The word gospel literally means “good news” and occurs 93 times in the Bible, exclusively in the New Testament. In Greek, it is the word euaggelion, from which we get our English words evangelist, evangel, and evangelical. The gospel is, broadly speaking, the whole of Scripture; more narrowly, the gospel is the good news concerning Christ and the way of salvation.

￼


The key to understanding the gospel is to know why it’s good news. To do that, we must start with the bad news. The Old Testament Law was given to Israel during the time of Moses (Deuteronomy 5:1). The Law can be thought of as a measuring stick, and sin is anything that falls short of “perfect” according to that standard. The righteous requirement of the Law is so stringent that no human being could possibly follow it perfectly, in letter or in spirit. Despite our “goodness” or “badness” relative to each other, we are all in the same spiritual boat—we have sinned, and the punishment for sin is death, i.e. separation from God, the source of life (Romans 3:23). In order for us to go to heaven, God’s dwelling place and the realm of life and light, sin must be somehow removed or paid for. The Law established the fact that cleansing from sin can only happen through the bloody sacrifice of an innocent life (Hebrews 9:22).

The gospel involves Jesus’ death on the cross as the sin offering to fulfill the Law’s righteous requirement (Romans 8:3–4; Hebrews 10:5–10). Under the Law, animal sacrifices were offered year after year as a reminder of sin and a symbol of the coming sacrifice of Christ (Hebrews 10:3–4). When Christ offered Himself at Calvary, that symbol became a reality for all who would believe (Hebrews 10:11–18). The work of atonement is finished now, and that’s good news.

The gospel also involves Jesus’ resurrection on the third day. “He was delivered over to death for our sins and was raised to life for our justification” (Romans 4:25). The fact that Jesus conquered sin and death (sin’s penalty) is good news, indeed. The fact that He offers to share that victory with us is the greatest news of all (John 14:19).

The elements of the gospel are clearly stated in 1 Corinthians 15:3–6, a key passage concerning the good news of God: “For what I received I passed on to you as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, and then to the Twelve. After that, he appeared to more than five hundred of the brothers and sisters at the same time, most of whom are still living.” Notice, first, that Paul “received” the gospel and then “passed it on”; this is a divine message, not a man-made invention. Second, the gospel is “of first importance.” Everywhere the apostles went, they preached the crucifixion and resurrection of Christ. Third, the message of the gospel is accompanied by proofs: Christ died for our sins (proved by His burial), and He rose again the third day (proved by the eyewitnesses). Fourth, all this was done “according to the Scriptures”; the theme of the whole Bible is the salvation of mankind through Christ. The Bible is the gospel.

“I am not ashamed of the gospel, because it is the power of God that brings salvation to everyone who believes: first to the Jew, then to the Gentile” (Romans 1:16). The gospel is a bold message, and we are not ashamed of proclaiming it. It is a powerful message, because it is God’s good news. It is a saving message, the only thing that can truly reform the human heart. It is a universal message, for Jews and Gentiles both. And the gospel is received by faith; salvation is the gift of God (Ephesians 2:8–9).

The gospel is the good news that God loves the world enough to give His only Son to die for our sin (John 3:16). The gospel is good news because our salvation and eternal life and home in heaven are guaranteed through Christ (John 14:1–4). “He has given us new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, and into an inheritance that can never perish, spoil or fade. This inheritance is kept in heaven for you” (1 Peter 1:3–4).

The gospel is good news when we understand that we do not (and cannot) earn our salvation; the work of redemption and justification is complete, having been finished on the cross (John 19:30). Jesus is the propitiation for our sins (1 John 2:2). The gospel is the good news that we, who were once enemies of God, have been reconciled by the blood of Christ and adopted into the family of God (Romans 5:10; John 1:12). “See what great love the Father has lavished on us, that we should be called children of God! And that is what we are!” (1 John 3:1). The gospel is the good news that “there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).

To reject the gospel is to embrace the bad news. Condemnation before God is the result of a lack of faith in the Son of God, God’s only provision for salvation. “For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but to save the world through him. Whoever believes in him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe stands condemned already because they have not believed in the name of God’s one and only Son” (John 3:17–18). God has given a doomed world good news: the Gospel of Jesus Christ!

300 lbs was my breaking point. I had previously lost 80lbs before on Weight Watchers with excessive energy drinks to force the exercise after work. It all came back. I've done boot camps and a pile of crash diets when i was younger, even naively bought green coffee pills as a teen at walmart. At 300 lbs I went to the clinic and asked to be put on the bariatric surgery waitlist. I worked in healthcare and knew the risks but I was at the end of my rope. 

The doctor advised me of the risks I already knew and worked with me to sort through the medication-based options vs my insurance. He gave me an rx and a sample pack of Contrave. For the first time, I feel full after in an appropriate amount of food is consumed. I'm not craving more or that 'always have room for dessert' feeling. My partner tries to share sweets with me, and I'm just not interested. It feels like how life should be, and probably is for normal people. Don't get me wrong, I'm having a multitude of side effects that can be quite uncomfortable, but i'll suffer through to help get me to a healthy weight where it'll be maintenance instead of the uphill battle I got myself into.

Unless you have been there, you have no idea whatsoever what the willpower to overcome the fork is like.  We were raised to finish our plates, because we didn't have anything and mom didn't want food wasted.  We're raised to eat when we can, because we're active and doing hard physical work, playing hard, etc.  Then - we turn into adults sitting in a chair typing at a keyboard.

The medication in this case can give people just that little bit more edge in the willpower department. Next, the diet really can change from just smaller portions to smaller, AND healthier choices.  Next think you know, the combination of the three is really working.

What do I know?  Experience is a great teacher, we'll just put it that way.

text: Very interesting video, thank you.  There is so much about weight loss/gain that we don't understand, and I don't think that it is a balance of calories in and calories out. text:
People need to wake up. This is not a miracle drug for weight loss. It is just a tool like with gastric bypass.

We don’t know enough about potential long term risks. You also likely can’t take it permanently, sooner or later the body might make it stop working, you or society might not be able to afford it, production might not meet demand and diabetes patients have to be prioritized, or production might stop altogether due to war or similar events.

Even on this drug, people need to change their lifestyles permanently, which includes diet, stopping with foods you can’t control and regular exercise.

People will regain all the weight and more when they’re forced to stop it for one reason or another. Do you think the 95% or so people losing weight gaining it back or more within a few years is a joke? Now you’re taking a drug that makes it unlikely that you truly change your lifestyle, relationship with food and gain experience with how to deal with it. 

The easy way is never the permanent or good way unless you make an effort to make up for what you lose for taking the easy route. Work with a dietician and so on to work out how to eat and get used to certain foods while making sure to stop eating some so you don’t get cravings for it easily.

I might’ve taken the drug if it came out 10-15 years earlier when I was younger and hadn’t learned how to actually lose weight permanently and be healthy, back then I just kept on failing because I didn’t know how important it was to make permanent changes nor how to keep it sustainable, I just went down in calories and never built up sustainable healthier habits. 

It’s a great drug but wake up and realize it’s not a miracle, has consequences and it’s not a set and forget kind of deal where you can just cheat yourself to a good, healthy life without real changes.

author: @V.C.R.11
text: I struggled with weight loss in my twenties but I'm not a pacient person so I decided to attack the root of the problem: my approach to food. Coming from a family where food is the thing you go to when anxious, when sad, when lonely, I've learned to give food a role it should have never had. I'm not an expert in the subject, just sharing my experience after two plus decades trying to loose weight in all the wrong ways and all the recommended ones. The only thing that resulted in a long term solution for me was to change my approach to food. It wasn't a matter of days but if you're consistent It changes your whole lifestyle. I don't see food anymore as a primary source of pleasure or comfort, I've replaced it with human connection, doing more of the things that nurture my soul and exercise. Exercise it's the best antistres and antidepressant I've ever had. I tried many types of exercises till i found the one i enjoy, so it doesn't feel like something I force myself to do, it's a pleasure. I truly believe there's an exercise for each type of person and most people give up before finding the one/s that they can enjoy. I don't prioritize anymore how food feels in my paladar either. I learned that the more condiments I use the more i eat, so i change what my paladar was used to. There's an old saying that became the golden premise for me: "We are animals of habit", so i knew that if I sustain the few changes i was able to implement for a while, at some point it would affect the intensity of my cravings and what i craved for too. It's even better if you do it step by step, it works anyway, as long as you're consistent. I don't think i did it the right way, i used a bunch of tricks. For example, I didn't quit all my bad eating habits, I chose the day of the week where most of the opportunities and temptations were around me to allow myself to eat whatever i felt like. For me that was Saturdays or Sundays with family around. The rest of the week I'd think of food just as fuel and nothing more. What happened is that, after a while, I didn't need to have as much of my cravings as i did before in order to feel satisfied, and as time passed by I was able to pass on the cravings, they lost the power they had on me before just by locking them up in a specific day of the week. Nowadays i don't even crave anymore things i thought i could never live without. It didn't happen from one day to the next one and i didn't know nor expected this to happen, I was just tricking myself in ways i thought i could sustain. As a result I'm convinced that the permanent solution it's to be willing to re-educate ourselves about our approach to food and the role we're assigning to it, and the right way to do it is nice and slow, giving time to our paladars, minds and bodies to learn new ways of getting what they need and new experiences of wellness and satisfaction. I never thought I could be the kind of person who eats one portion of anything and be satisfied, but time did the trick. At the beginning i cheated with diet sodas in order to feel full, then i discovered that having fatty meats, nuts and avocados made me feel full faster and for longer hours. In time my stomach reduced and now I can have whatever i want without abusing it, because it's just food, it's not my maine source of pleasure or comfort. There are so many other activities that can nurture us and provide us of all those things we tend to wrongly seek for in food...and you don't need to be rich to implement a few changes in your lifestyle, it's more about being willing to learn new ways of experiencing your life.

author: @vohkaru131
text:
It's wild how even a medical professional can think the root cause of somebody being 400 lbs is the lack of a morning jog.

Annoyed. Gotta rant. Here is why people fail, and also how to succeed:

The common messaging around weight loss boils down to this: Stop consuming the things you enjoy, stick to sallads and lean meats, and start exercising. This oversimplifies how weight management actually works to the point where any individual who is not already super motivated is going to feel like losing weight is a herculean task. It leads to unrealistic expectations of how many calories exercise actually burns, it leads to crash dieting which puts the body in starvation mode and in doing so it royally ramps up appetite and hunger, and it doesn't take into account the psychology surrounding compulsive eating. In other words, it sets people up to fail.

Successful weight management is more comprehensive and detailed:

1. You have to account for how food is used as a coping mechanism for emotional distress. You can try to attack it through introspective meditation, going to therapy, finding new interests, and/or finding lower calorie substitutes. The important thing here is to not just suddenly stop eating the things you like before you've actually addressed the underlying issue, otherwise you'll just leave yourself more miserable, and misery is what drives overconsumption.

author: @rossmurray6849
text:
There is one danger in using these drugs that wasn't mentioned in this video. Many people regain the weight they've lost once they stop taking the drug. That would appear to end up back where they started but that is often not so. When going through that people will tend to lose some fat and some muscle on the way down, but put on mostly fat as they regain weight. The loss of muscle mass as a proportion of total weight means they can be substantially less healthy than when at the same weight as before started. 
That said, I am delighted and amazed at the results of using this drug PLUS some moderate but regular weight sessions in the gym. It is worth noting too that the same caution applies for ALL methods of losing weight, i.e. unless efforts are made to preserve muscle mass while losing weight you'll end up less healthy than before if you return back to your starting weight.

author: @lokipokey
text:
Most of the studies on weight regain after stopping these drugs involved taking the patient to top the maximum level of the drug for at least 6 to 12 months and then cutting them off cold turkey.
However a few studies have involved titrating the dose down slowly over time, and also continuing dietitian and exercise support. In those cases, the majority of patients maintain their weight loss. If they continued the drug, they did so at a very low dose. 
Also, we are learning that taking the maximum dose is not always necessary. Good obesity doctors are recommending that patients take no higher of a dose than is necessary to lose weight at a reasonable rate.
I lost 50 lb using tirzepatide over the course of a year, which is less than a pound a week. I ate plenty of protein and did lots of weight-bearing exercise.
Less than 10% of my weight loss was lean body mass, the rest was fat.
I never went above 2/3 of the maximum dose and that only for a few months. Mostly I was on half the maximum dose. 
Now that I'm at goal weight, I've been titrating down and have maintained for about 6 weeks. 
The medical community is learning more about these drugs as time goes on, but I think the approach that my doctor and I have used will turn out to be more effective long-term. He says that the vast majority of his patients are on the minimum dose, a microdose, or have managed to titrate completely off of the drugs.

text: I'm diabetic and obese at 59 yo. I couple Mounjaro use with a Keto diet and intermittent fasting. With any weight-loss program, there's always an alarm about "muscle loss," but much of what is happening is one is losing fluids and inflammation in one's muscles, not muscle tissue itself (making muscular folks appear to have shrinking muscle, but the pure muscle mass is not being consumed by the weight loss). The body turns to its fat reserves so long as insulin (weight gaining hormone) is kept low, and leptin (weight loss hormone) is allowed to elevate, as when one is in ketosis. I have also been reversing my diabetes completely. I'm at the level of prediabetes now (A1C from 11.0 in June 2024 to 5.8 in December 2024). This saved my life and from future miseries of diabetic afflictions in old age. I also read that even if one puts aside exercise, a great cause of many diseases is a lack of sunlight and abundant fresh oxygen. So, I have also undertaken to take my dog on long daily walks (giving us both exercise) and breathing in the fresh air (oxygen is an enemy to cancers) and robustly increasing my vitamin D with sunlight exposure. I experience no side effects from Mounjaro. I now take 10 mL once a week (having moved up from 2.5, 5.0, and 7.5 mL). I stay at my current does as long as it still feels effective in suppressing my appetite, especially at night - my worse time to overeat.

author: @alyssam.5939
text:
I just came back from a two-month trip to Japan. What I noticed there is that very few people are overweight, and I didn't see anyone who appeared morbidly obese. Japan has one of the lowest obesity rates in the world. What is different there? The food supply and food culture. Granted, there are some unhealthy aspects of their food culture with a focus on thinness, but there is a reason their obesity rates are so low. It starts in childhood: schools have a dietician on staff and food is made from scratch daily. It's real food, unlike food fed to kids at school in the U.S., for example. As for adults, the serving sizes are small, you simply don't eat while walking around - you basically eat at meals, unsweetened drinks are very common, people eat more real food plus fermented foods, they walk a lot more, and even the processed food contains significantly less sugar than the food in my country (the U.S.). While I was there, I lost eight pounds. 

The problem with the GLP-1 medications is that it's not addressing the root issues of the obesity epidemic. It's taking a systemic, cultural and food supply issue seen mostly in the U.S. but also now in the in U.K., Australia, and Canada, and turning it into an individual issue that can be addressed by taking a medication in order to eat less. The reason our hunger cues are so messed up in the first place is that food companies have gotten rich off of creating "frankenfood" that is highly addictive and hardly recognized as food by our bodies and brains. They have made our food highly-processed and highly palatable while pumping this "food" full of sugar, fat, and salt, all of which has rewired our brains and made us addicted. The more we eat, the more money they make. This is why this medication will not solve the obesity issue because it is not addressing the root problem. Once people go off the medication, many, if not most, will gain much of the weight back. Unfortunately, people are getting rich from pushing this medication as a "wonder drug" for the obesity issue; however, this is not just an individual issue but a societal problem.

text:
We don't have the studies and data to know what the potential long term health risks are for Ozempic in bodies that have a functioning pancreas. It was a diabetes medication. And yet big Pharma has pushed this as if theres many 10-year doubleblind studies on it with positive outcomes. We dont know. We DONT. Studies have been small and not long enough for any definitive data. I looked into it before I started my own health voyage and declined to use it. 
But Big Farma makes billions from it and thats THEIR gold standard. 

I dont personally work in the emergency department of the hosptial but nurses and doctors that do have told me theyve seen an influx in the last year alone of patients presenting with pancreatitis (NECROTIC pancreatitis even) and gastroperesis that was caused directly by Ozempic, Wegovy, etc. 

Its NOT a risk free drug and we are also now seeing that those who discontinue it regain the weight within a year at far too high numbers for the benefits to outweigh the risks in my opinion. 

And before the group of ignoramouses come for me, I'm not gatekeeping thinness or fatphobic. I was very obese up until recently with a host of medical problems including prediabetes, high cholesterol, PCOS and that good stuff. I faced my addiction with food and implemented a lifestyle change eith a calorie deficit coupled with exercise and documenting what inwas eating. I no longer have any of those issues and im off all medications. It is brutal, depressing, arduous and difficult with many ups and downs. Ozempic will not cure the psycbological drive to eat when it comes to a food problem. Its merely masking it until its discontinued and then eventually youre back to square one. I had to face it and treat the problem that was in my mind and mindset. I still have to tackle it every day. Its been a two year journey but I finally feel like im in a good place now outwardly and inwardly. Ozempic cannot fix my mind and will not fix what led me to be as bad off as I was. Its not a magic shot. But nobody wants to hear that. They get big mad and offended. I dont care.

text:
What scares me about these extreme measures, are how many people are willing to take the 'easy' solution - without any thought of the side effects. And how much doctors seem to market these things. Before Ozempic, it was weight loss surgery. 

These things should only be used as a last resort, when it can't be done naturally. Not as the recommended solution. Because it comes with side effects and potentially life long consequences. While so much can actually be helped naturally.

What we should be doing, is to make everyone responsible for living a reasonably healthy lifestyle from birth. Everyone should have a responsibility to live a reasonably healthy and active life, to prevent lifestyle diseases. To support this, there should be education, even for children, on a healthy lifestyle. And workplaces should also support these things to a certain extent. It will teach people to love their body and what it can do, and enjoy physical activity and healthy, delicious foods. I am not talking extremes in any way - just learning the balance.

If we did this, just think about how many people would not need health care, or would need less of it. It would impact everything from physical conditions, to mental health. And all the resources used in the healthcare system could be used on people who actually need it.

author: @PaulWilsonGroup
text:
Wow! This is not journalism. Why?

1. Transparency and Objectivity
The segment introduces Roy Webster and his tragic story. Still, it does not provide substantial verification of the claims made about the drug Ozempic's role in Trish's death. There is a heavy reliance on personal anecdotes without enough corroborating medical opinions or data.
The segment seems to focus heavily on the adverse outcomes associated with Ozempic without giving equal weight to its approved medical uses and benefits for diabetic patients. It features dramatic personal stories and negative expert opinions, which can skew the audience's perception.
2. Sensationalism
The narrative is emotionally charged, with dramatic descriptions of Trish's death and the impact on her family. This emotional appeal could be seen as an attempt to sensationalize the story rather than provide a balanced view.
The use of phrases like "fat-burning Revolution" and "wonder drug" without sufficient evidence can contribute to sensationalism. The segment might oversimplify the complexities of the drug's effects and its regulatory status.
3. Accuracy and Fairness
The connection between Ozempic and the deaths discussed is not clearly established with robust medical evidence. To avoid misrepresentation, the segment should have included more detailed and scientifically backed information.
While the segment does mention regulatory warnings and lawsuits, it does not thoroughly explore the reasons behind these actions or the scientific context. There is also a need for more discussion on the prevalence of side effects relative to the number of users.
4. Minimizing Harm
The portrayal of Ozempic might lead viewers to fear the drug without fully understanding its benefits and risks. This could deter patients from using a medication that could benefit them under proper medical supervision.
The segment should have balanced the personal stories concerning the individuals involved and the broader public interest. It's essential to show compassion while providing a clear, factual account of the situation.

The "60 Minutes" segment on Ozempic falls short of several vital journalistic ethics principles:
Transparency: Insufficient identification and verification of sources and their claims.
Objectivity: A biased presentation that heavily leans towards the negative aspects of the drug without providing a balanced view.
Sensationalism: Use of emotional appeals and exaggerated claims that could mislead the audience.
Accuracy and Fairness: Lack of robust medical evidence and nuanced context.
Minimizing Harm: Potential to cause unwarranted fear among viewers regarding a medication that can be beneficial when used correctly.

A professional journalist can strive for balanced reporting, transparent sourcing, and a focus on factual, evidence-based information. But then again, sometimes the truth doesn't make for good ratings and advertising revenue.

author: @jaspercarmack
text:
Sharing my experience; 

I lived through Bupropion (stimulant medication induced) bowel obstruction/gastroparesis and it was the single most dreadful experience of my life; absolutely foul horrid disgusting tasting burps were the warning sign that preceded it, yet when I saw a doctor, they kept just dismissing it as "probably a bit of acid reflux.". The hospitals were like"oh you probably just ate something that didn't agree with you". Their opinion changed when I passed out in the toilet with jets shooting out both ends while I was unconscious.

I am bloody lucky to have lived, but I am extremely frustrated that even in the face of this investigation, no one is mentioning the ABSOLUTELY CRUCIAL warning sign: The foul tasting burps. They are not mentioned anywhere in any form of medical literature, nor mentioned anywhere as a side effect of Ozempic or Stimulant drugs. Yet if you go and check patient reviews for these drugs or have a quick google around, you'll see that whilst it's of low incidence, it is absolutely under-reported.

My gastroenterologist told me; "If you ever encounter this symptom (the foul burps) again, you MUST go straight to hospital". He was right.

The diarrhea was severe and akin to magnesium citrate (colonoscopy prep) does to you, but about three times more frequent. The vomiting was unstoppable and dry retching continued even after my stomach was empty. The nausea was bad enough to put me into shock. I ended up dehydrated so severely that I suffered Acute Renal Injury (Kidney failure). The doctors treated the kidney failure, but when I mentioned the diarrhea/burps etc, they just gave me a blank stare and repeated the same answer as before; "Oh you probably have a bit of acid reflux.".

Back then (And even today it seems) the horrid taste/smell of the burps is majorly overlooked and ignored. They're not just "a bit off", they are the worst tasting/smelling burps in the world, unlike anything I've ever encountered; it's worse than roadkill, worse than a sewer, worse than death, and it comes up nonstop and you cannot stop it. If you go and have a read online at people taking this drug (or stimulant drugs, which were the cause of mine), you'll see it's extremely frequent, yet listed absolutely nowhere in any medical notation?

The reason this key symptom is important is that; when you present to the ER with just "nausea, vomiting, diarrhea", it could be about one of a million different health conditions, however the most common causes of these is things like a stomach virus/bacterial infection, alcohol use, etc. I believe that my gastroenterologist was correct; if doctors use the taste/smell as a criteria (and believe you me, you will KNOW when you experience them; they come out unstoppably and the taste and smell is unlike anything on this planet, it is outright scary how bad it is), they could use this to intervene early.

I’ve been on Tirzepatide (Mounjaro and now Zepbound) for 78 weeks.  I eat MORE than I have in the last 18 years having been dieting and exercising my way (to exhaustion mind you) to gaining over 100 pounds. author: @bettypearson5570
text:
Ozempic is great for losing 15-20% of your body weight if you don't suffer side effects, some of which are severe, and the fact that the only way you will keep it off you have to stay on it for life.

But what if you weigh 300 pounds?  Then you will lose around 60 pounds at most.  Very exciting at the beginning as it comes off so quickly.  Unfortunately, that still leaves you  at 240 pounds which is there to stay.  Unless you are a 6'6" man that still means you are still obese and still are stuck with the side effects and still putting out the money each month.  Are you going to be happy still being fat?

I had gotten up to 411 sporadically going on diets which usually resulted in a loss between 5-10 pounds before getting discouraged and quitting while gaining it all back plus a few extra.

What changed was when I found out about a study which indicated drinking whole milk was better for weight loss than non fat milk plus it tastes better.  I switched and I dramatically decreased my favorite veggies which turned out to be the highest in oxalates which I had many symptoms of having difficulty processing.  Because milk and other dairy bonds with the oxalates and I was drinking lots of milk I stopped passing kidney stones and having gout attacks.

As an added bonus, without trying I lost 15 pounds the first month and in the next 2 months lost another 12.

A couple months after I slowed to a stop and decided to add in a high fat and protein keto type diet.  Couldn't give up veggies or all sugar just yet. But over the next couple months lost another 30 for a total of 57 pounds taking me down to 364.  At that weight the benefit was feeling a little better physically but not enough that others noticed.  By starting with a few steps that didn't really require self control or depriving myself much. It got me started.  I just continued tweaking little changes when I was able to maintain my loss instead of regaining for a couple weeks.  I am now down to 232; still obese but enough to notice.  I've dropped from size 30 to size 18 and still going without the side effects and not only no extra cost but reduced cost because of less food to buy.

No regrets for not using ozempic and I've lost more than I ever would have on the drug.

text:
So much of what’s being said here is misinformation. Ozempic isn’t a miracle drug, and it’s not meant to be a free pass to overeat. It’s a tool that works best when combined with lifestyle changes like balanced nutrition, exercise, and good sleep.

Many side effects people talk about (especially digestive ones) are more common when diet quality doesn’t improve. Eating nutrient-dense foods (lean proteins, fruits, and vegetables) in reasonable portions usually makes a huge difference. Titration is also key: starting at a low dose and gradually increasing helps the body adjust.

For people who use Ozempic alongside healthy choices, the reality is often very different from what’s being sensationalized and most report little to no side effects and steady, sustainable progress.

Ozempic is dangerous!

I had received 1 more unit of blood (for a total of 7 units in 2 weeks) just to bring me back up to a hemoglobin of 9. I was discharged a week later. I have no memory of the first two days after becoming unconscious. Then 6 weeks later my hemoglobin was down to 6.1 and again I was hospitalized for 6 days after another life flight from my local hospital. I wish I had stayed with it instead of listening to the Wegovy and Ozempic commercials for quicker weight loss.

author: @kristendaniels5656
text: As a general rule I keep silent when I am watching you do other videos. But with this, I need to speak up. Some people may be raging mad at me and that’s OK. But if what I say gives at least one person pause before considering these medications then it will be worth it.  Whether it is Ozempic or Wegovy, the fact remains that the side effects of these medications should not be dismissed. I have personally witnessed these side effects on a friend of mine. First, I want to  start off by saying that she was a metformin controlled diabetic. Her starting weight before her doctor suggested Ozempic was 225 pounds. She definitely lost the weight in a drastic amount of time, but not a day went by where she wasn’t Vomiting at least five times a day. And that was just our eight hour shift working together. God only knows how often this was happening at home. I begged her to stop and told her that this wasn’t healthy and this was not normal. But she pushed through because her doctor said that the side effects would subside eventually. But it never did. She called her doctor and told him what was going on. He dismissed it and said don’t worry about it. It’s just a side effect and that it would eventually pass. Well, it didn’t pass and she has been hospitalized multiple times for dehydration and malnourishment. The excessive vomiting has caused damage to her throat because of how acidic vomit is, she will be having surgery soon because of the gastroparesis that she developed because of it . Due to this medication, it has caused part of her intestine to literally die, and now that needs to be removed, followed by a colostomy bag. I don’t know if it’s temporary or if it’s going to be permanent. As of the end of March 2025 of this year, there are almost 1700 active Personal lawsuits because of the gastroparesis that Ozempic has caused. I know these  people will never get a payout because they were willing participants. These pharmaceutical companies needed willing human participants to truly see the side effects of this medication. (Much like the medication they push on the trans community, but I digress).These pharmaceutical companies have enough money and legal representation to keep this held up in court as long as they want to. People have been chasing the magical cure for weight loss for forever. Hell back in the turn of the century people were swallowing tapeworms to lose weight. So it’s no different. But I do hold pharmaceutical companies and physicians responsible for pushing the snake oil rather than encouraging a nutritionist as well as a mental health professional. And the reason why they don’t do this… Is because there’s no money to be had for the pharmaceutical company or for the doctors. Doctors and drug companies create a vicious cycle that will never end to make money and that is an absolute fact. Medications  can cure or hold an illness at Bay, but it can also create a whole new host of problems that need more medication. And the fact that these people are pushing medication used for legitimate diabetics is disgusting. The medical community is choosing vanity over somebody who truly needs this medication. Weight loss is not easy. I am 52 years old and weigh 210 pounds. But I will be damned if I shove a pill down my throat or inject myself with a medication as a quick fix. Sometimes you just have to soul search to find out the root cause of over eating And obesity. It could be that you just need to stay away from processed foods and the Hoho’s  in the snack aisle. But for others, it could be trauma that they suffered through that they need to address. Please know that I am writing this post out of love. There is no malice or maliciousness behind any of my words. I am just begging people to reconsider before going down this path.

Cholesterol begins to build up plaque in your arteries, including your carotid arteries, placing you at HIGH RISK for strokes, heart attacks, high blood pressure, and other cardiovascular diseases or events. 

Being on a Ketogenic diet is also very acidic, which eats away at the minerals in your bones - moreso if you are not doing healthy Keto, which requires 7-10 cups of vegetables daily. This can lead to a rapid deterioration of your bone density, resulting in osteopenia and osteoporosis, also VERY difficult to reverse, taking YEARS, IF reversible all.

Then, in your ignorant, faddish behavior, all the doctors can to do is medicate you and pile on the medications (for cholesterol, high blood pressure, osteoporosis, etc.) as symptoms shoot off in a cadence, which in themselves bring side effects, more diseases and more medications. 

Extra calcium supplements for your bones can lead to calcium deposits in your arteries and organs, especially kidneys, leading to greater arterial blockage, kidney stones and kidney disease.  Osteoporosis medication makes your bones brittle so that they shatter instead of fracture. 

Speaking from EXPERIENCE. With Keto, within 1 to 2 years, you can RUIN your health. Don't be lazy. Don't be ignorant. Don't just listen to internet gurus cashing in views on youtube from brain-fogged people looking for easy fixes (I was one of them). DO YOUR HOMEWORK.

Above all, get all your medical exams done, keep a close periodic check on them for prevention, and consult your Doctor and LICENSED nutritionist regularly. They can spot early detection of health impacts and they can help you lose weight without ruining your health.

Having a balanced amount of carbs for energy allows your body to send the other macros to where they need to go: protein to your muscles, fat to its respective functions, etc. Just eat balanced, natural (i.e., organic, unprocessed), healthy and in proportionate moderation. Exercise, sleep (control and minimise caffeine intake), and learn to manage stress, as cortisol is a major culprit in weight gain issues, as well as other hormone imbalances from improper sleep. See Dr. Matthew Walker (UC Berkeley) and Dr. Andrew Huberman (Stanford) for more on this.

Keto may be used successfully on people already sick with neurological disorders, to improve their quality of life amid seizures. However, Keto does sicken otherwise healthy people, and in many cases (if you look at charts published on the death rates, age at death and causes of death of Keto/Adkins low carb gurus), we can clearly see that it can lead to premature death.

text:
Ladies and gentlemen,

Today, I stand before you to address a topic that holds immense significance in our lives—losing weight. I want to ignite a spark within each one of you, a flame of determination that will guide you on your journey towards a healthier and happier you.

First, let me emphasize that this journey is not about conforming to society's standards of beauty or succumbing to external pressures. It is about reclaiming your vitality, enhancing your well-being, and nurturing your self-confidence. Remember, you are embarking on this path for yourself and no one else.

In this quest, it's essential to understand that weight loss is not a quick fix or a temporary phase. It requires patience, consistency, and a commitment to adopting healthy habits. Set realistic goals and celebrate each milestone you achieve. Remember, progress is not measured solely by numbers on a scale but by the positive changes you make in your life.

Embrace the power of self-love and self-care. Treat your body as a temple, nourishing it with wholesome foods and engaging in physical activities that bring you joy. Explore different forms of exercise, find what resonates with you, and make it a regular part of your routine. Remember, it's not about punishment; it's about embracing a healthier lifestyle.

In this journey, setbacks and obstacles are inevitable. There will be days when motivation wanes, when temptations arise, and when self-doubt creeps in. But remember, you possess a reservoir of strength within you that is capable of conquering any challenge. Surround yourself with a support system of loved ones who uplift and inspire you. Seek guidance from professionals who can provide you with the knowledge and tools necessary for success.

But most importantly, believe in yourself. Believe that you have the power to transform your life, to break free from the chains that have held you back. Believe that every choice you make towards your health and well-being is a step towards a brighter future.

You are worthy of the best version of yourself—vibrant, confident, and full of life. Remember, this journey is not about reaching an endpoint but about embracing a lifelong commitment to your well-being.

So, my friends, as you embark on this transformative path, let inspiration guide your every step. Let the desire for a healthier, happier life be the fuel that propels you forward. And may you find strength, resilience, and unwavering determination within yourself to overcome every obstacle that comes your way.

Believe in the power of your dreams, for today is the day you take control of your life and create a future filled with health, vitality, and endless possibilities.

Thank you.
