text: TO lose the weight IS possible, i was on my 3rd ankle surgery xmas  2010 and the last thing i wanted to hear when my surgeon came and saw me after recovery was, [we have done our best with you ankle but next time its an ankle fusion and that will be soon if you dont make some life changes and do something about your weight ] .I weighted 268lbs  and was 5ft6in tall my weight had ballooned as my mobility had gone down, i was in plaster casts and braces until  March 2011, then as soon as i got my cast of and started physio i went low carb /atkins by the end of September 2011 i was going on holiday as a treat to Florida and i weighted in at 198lbs i had lost the weight with JUST my diet, as exercise is not my friends with my physical issues, besides my foot i have hip and back issues . By xmas 2011 my weight was down 172lbs  and i got to my lowest at my one year mark 162lbs . its been over 10 years since i started this journey and its not easy, i am now low carb through the week and treats at weekends i have gained 15lbs over the last 10 years from when i got to my lowest. BUT then  covid19 became the new norm so at the moment i am 179lbs . MY advise take the journey slow dont get down on yourself if you dont hit a target,  you are going to be in this for the long hall and the best thing to help that is to realize that things are going to suck, but that once you started just keep going .HOPE YOU GET TO YOUR GOAL KEEP POSITIVE .

text: Your story is inspiring. I was in a similar situation. In April 2024, I remember looking at myself in the mirror and being ashamed of myself for letting my body get to the point that I was around 300 pounds. I made a vow to end bad eating habits, cutting out fast food, all sodas, refined sugars and processed meats. I incorporated vegetables into each meal as well as ate almost entirely turkey breast or chicken breast with an occasional sirloin steak for added protein. I bought a rowing machine, a treadmill and later an exercise bike and allotted 30-90 minutes every day to exercising. If I couldn't exercise in the morning, I did so in the evening when I got off work. author: @lkeilitz1989
text:
I began my weight loss journey 2wks ago at 368lbs. I was a truck driver for over a decade. My diet sucked (mostly fast food and restaurants) and virtually zero exercise (mostly driving 10-11hrs a day, walking to/from the truck at truck stops/warehouses, and sleeping). Given, I would try to eat the healthier meals like grilled fish, rice, and a veggie at restaurants. I was taking in 2000+ calories and maybe using around 900-1300. Since leaving that career in 2022, I have not been very active. I’ll go on a hike in a local park every once in a while but have never committed to a daily cardio or exercise routine. That is all about to change!

2wks ago I decided to start my journey by making small changes to my diet. I cut sugar and starches by giving up soda, junk food, breads, noodles, etc. I have also reduced my portions by about half of the massive plates I used to serve myself. In just two weeks, this simple change has resulted in a loss of 14lbs down to 354lbs. I have replaced typical sugar-packed deserts with fruits and replaced starchy/fatty sides with veggies. Those few changes are already having a positive effect and I haven’t added any exercises yet. My plan is to start Monday by adding 30min of entry-level Yoga and a 2 mile walk every other day. Once that becomes routine/habit I will add more exercises or longer times/distances to the Yoga and walking. 

Unfortunately, I am a smoker so I do not see myself “training for a 5k” or doing other intense cardio anytime soon. I have tried every method of quitting (gum, patches, medication) to no avail. The problem is that I am more addicted to the aesthetics (watching the cigarette burn brighter/watching the smoke) than the nicotine. For some reason, those things are very soothing/calming to me.

Either way, I’m hoping that as I practice a combination of portion control, cutting sugar/starches/bad cholesterol, eating more fruits/veggies/healthy meats, committing to walking everyday, practicing yoga, weight training, and doing some other light cardio that my lungs can handle I will begin to feel better/lose weight faster. As I lose weight and gain energy I may reach a point where I will be comfortable with quitting smoking. If/when that happens, I know I will reach a point of health/happiness in my life that I haven’t experienced since I was 20 (I’m 36 now). If anyone has any advice or stories they want to share, please do.

text:
Been struggling with weight myself for a long time. I also tried different things and would go in 100%, but it's very hard to keep doing things you hate.

Now I'm doing just small things that are easy to do. Eating less snacks, in fact no snacking during the week, but it's fine on weekends. No soda, stop eating when you're full and a bit more walking. I've only been doing it for a month, but so far I've lost 5kg/11lbs and it's been relatively easy. Definitely something I can keep doing for many more months.

If you're watching this and want to loose some weight yourself, do some small things that you know you can keep on doing. Try it for a week, a month or 3 months, just to see where it brings you.

text:
I work with this (very fit and attractive) middle aged woman who swears by the mindset: Just stay consistent. Life is about building habits. We end up out of shape because we build habits that result in being out of shape. 

Look around you and it’s obvious there are people who have built habits around being IN shape. There will be days that you just don’t want to go to the gym, you just don’t want to eat healthy. But just stay consistent, make it a habit. That will make it THAT much easier to do the healthy thing even if you don’t want to, in the moment. If your brain and body expects to go to the gym more often than not, it’ll make it so much easier to get yourself there on the days you feel “off.” 

That’s all it is, just changing your habits. Hard to break a cycle, but hey we do it all the time with drugs, alcohol, food, etc. Just make yourself commit.

text: I've lost over 100 pounds and here is one of the main things I learned. Stop thinking about timelines. Most of the time people say they want to lose X amount of weight in X amount of time. Why? text:
The most inspiring thing is how you grew your arm back! 😂 


JK! I’m an idiot… Sorry! 😂😂😂 But seriously, great job! 
Personally, I used to be on a vegetarian/daily intermittent fasting diet (fruit and veg, only healthy fats and carbs, only whole grains, no processed sugar, no caffeine etc) and I felt so much better!!! In addition, I was a healthy weight. But most important to me was how much better I felt….More energy, better sleep, less depression, less “woman” issues, less muscle pain  etc.  It wasn’t too long before I just didn’t crave anything else and I was never hungry outside of my eating window. But over time, a busy life, having to constantly prepare what was essentially two different dinners (hubby and kids were not vegetarians), boredom due to restricted flavor options (really because I didn’t have the time to put in the effort to learn how to try new things) and social pressures ( people outside the family constantly bringing up my dietary decisions) got me off track. Then the pandemic hit and I gave up completely since selective food shopping became increasingly difficult. All my health issues came back. I have been struggling to get back on the horse for, what feels like, an eternity.  I have finally ( I hope) gotten to where I can’t stand feeling sick, having zero energy, and being in pain anymore. As a side note, I’ve always had a relatively fast metabolism so I’ll gain 30 pounds or so and then work to drop it ( mostly just by restricting my diet for a while and with the help of certain meds that curb my appetite…a pleasant side effect but that’s not what I take them for…perhaps you you can tell by my style of commenting that the ADHD is strong with this one!!!😂😂😂.) So I never have gotten to what could really be called “overly obese”, but it runs in my family to become so as we get older… (and I’m definitely getting older) 😂…so dropping the extra weight is becoming harder. But I carry the weight in a way that I can hide a lot of it with the right clothing and so I get funny looks from people who are heavier than me when I say I need to lose weight. I think I, and maybe everyone, should change the language to, “I need to get healthy.” Regardless of weight, I’m still propping myself up with caffeine, sugar, fats, carbs and medication just to get through the day, and then I crash …HARD… sometimes for days at a time. I’m sick of feeling like crap! Being thinner and looking “good” really should just be an added bonus. So…I’m now scouring YouTube for inspiration. I know what works for me. I just need to believe I can do it again. And the withdrawal is a BEAST! I will have to go through mad headaches and emotional turmoil to get off the caffeine and sugar! NOT FUN!!!
But anywho, thanks for the video! Sorry for the long, rambling, ADHD fueled, and grammatically infuriating comment. (I’m just hoping that by adding my experience to the discussion, someone who may be in a similar boat, can benefit somehow.) 
And so glad to see that you were able to regrow that arm!!!!!😂😂😂

author: @CassondraWolf-hs3vh
text:
All great tips. All of this becomes a lifestyle and second nature when you do it for long enough. If you don’t have underlying conditions, losing weight is physically very easy, it’s a mental journey though. I changed my thought process from using food as reward to using it strictly as fuel and if you can make that fuel taste good that’s even better! 
I make sure to get a shit tonne of protein in the morning so I’m satiated throughout the day. 
I drink my protein shake right before bed because it gives me indigestion but I don’t notice when I’m sleeping. 
Switch your favourite foods for low fat, protein fortified, low calorie options. 
My coach said if you aren’t willing to eat a plate of broccoli you’re having a craving, you’re not hungry. 
If you don’t have it in your house you are less likely to eat it. 
Don’t forget your “why”. It’s not about what you eat in a day but what you eat in a week. 
Lost 50lb after my first two babies but got really sick with my third. Trying to remember how good it felt to stick to it and see results. It feels better to make gains than eat a bag of chips.

A lil advice from a 43kg salvic girl 😆 -drink real milk, it’s not supposed to be low calories, find where to get real butter, who cares how many calories there is in it, you don’t eat half of the pack in one day anyways. But you’re gonna eat good and healthy products. 
-I love real peanut butter but the one that has no sugar or added sweeteners in it. I eat it a lot. Ofc yall don’t have to eat the same amount of it as I do. Especially cause it’s not sweet. But I love to eat it with sugar free salty crackers omggg😭😭  
-Also I eat fried food, just use olive oil or better coconut oil. And ofc don’t eat fried food every day. For bread, I don’t eat it every day, and most of the times I use buckwheat crisp breads for sandwiches instead of bread. 
-Also drink more water and green tea. Add some ginger in it, it helps your digestion. Don’t lay down after you eat. 
- I don’t drink soda at all. And I never add sugar in my tea or coffee. It’s easy to get rid of sugar when it comes to liquids 😆 after like a week or so your gonna think that people who drink tea with sugar or drink soda are crazy cause it’s all toooo sweet 🥴 
Hope it helps yall ❤️

text:
I have three tips to add that is currently helping me:
 1. Go to the doctor and get blood work done. You may be eating something you think is healthy, but not healthy for you; everyone is different. They can also tell you if you have an intolerant that would be counterproductive. 

2. Fruit that you can hold in your hand (whole fruit) is a good way to kick a sugar craving and add fiber, which makes you feel full for a long time: apples, bananas, pears, plums, peaches, oranges, etc. 

3. Make an overall choice to be healthier and feel better. Let weight loss be a receipt of your new efforts. This way whether you lose a lot of weight or a little, you'll be better than you were and possibly live longer to experience the change. After all, you have forever to get it together!

author: @SLPurser
text:
We need to understand the difference between re-creation and escape.
When we recreate, we re-create ourselves: our mental strength, physical strength, our ability to cope.  
We return better able to face our challenges. (Find activities that do that for you).
But when we escape, we are just running away from life.  We do some indulgent activity, (sleep, chocolate, binge watch something) then return no better to face life than when we "escaped."
Certainly there are times when we need to just escape, but a balanced life should focus more on re-creating than on escape.

author: @jkp62
text: I found I just had to start and that was by walking 15 minutes per day- I set my phone alarm to 7 1/2 minutes and when it alarmed, I turned around to go home, every day, each week I added 5 minutes until I reached 1 hour (30 minutes out and 30 minutes back). Then researched low carb foods and low glycemic foods (after I started walking I was told I was pre-diabetic), got rid of white stuff first like rice, pasta, potatoes and bread, yes it was a struggle but my health was more important than my cravings., I noticed a big difference in 3 weeks by cutting those white things out like no bloat, minimal gas, no cravings for those items or even sweet stuff. More research brought me to make half my plate low carb/glycemic vegetables, 1/4 my protein and the other 1/4 a starch or fruit. My weight started going down, my A1C dropped to 4.9 from 8.6 and I felt better, slept better and had more energy and focus. It’s just doing it that’s the hardest. And I only weigh myself about everyone months at the doctor’s to do follow up stuff for my A1C and high blood pressure; my first noticeable change besides my face was I had to tighten my watch band, then it was tightening my belt by one hole, etc, then I noticed my shirts fit looser, I needed new bras and underwear, then my pants were looser, especially in the thigh and calves. All I did was walk and change food around and stop eating after 5 pm, now I strength train to tone muscle and build bone density. Life is so much better!

9) Write down your favourite foods and check GI. She plans for her favourite foods and incorporates them daily.

text:
If you want to lose weight and keep it off you need to cut down on the carbs, sugar and vegetable/seed oils.

Just keep it simple, keep insulin low and eat whole food:
- Eliminate sugar 
- Eat till you're full
- ↓Carbohydrate 
- Meat, veggies & fat
- ↓Procesed food 
- ↑Healthy fat (tallow/lard/butter/ghee)

The following ratios are ideal:
15% protein 
80% fat
5% carbohydrates 

Daily you should also spend as many hours doing physical exersice/sports as you do sitting in front of the TV. For example: if you spent half an hour working outside in the garden you can spend half an hour in front of the TV, if you spent an hour riding your bike you can spend an hour in front of the TV, etc.

author: @drzpapi413
text:
I've lost 90+ pounds 4 times. 
My efforts at the gym come easy, but dieting does not. When I lock in, I can drop weight but keeping it off is the challenge. Why? Because I fall for the good foods and bad foods mindset, so when I give in to a cookie, I say F it and go on a 7,000 calorie binge. I've started a new journey and here's what I changed. No foods are bad they just all come with a different cost. Now here's the actionable trick that has helped me in this new journey; I looked up my Basal Metabolic Rate. 2,600. So I diet on about 1,400 calories for 2 days. If I feel great (meaning no cravings or not feeling lethargic) I'll go a 3rd day at 1,400. I then follow that with a 2,400 caloric intake for 1 day and after drop back down to 1,400 and repeat. This has been a game changer. Hopes this helps that one person who can kind of resonate with my story. 
Started: 314lbs 
Currently:297lbs
Goal: 210lbs
First week dropped 8lbs. 
Second week dropped 9lbs. 
I'm running OMAD. High protein, moderate fats, low carbs. No not keto lol. 
ACV 2x a day. MCT Oil before training. 
Weight lifting and stair master for cardio. 
Remember, the minute you transform your mentality and lifestyle, your body did as well it just takes some time to show. So be happy. Because you're being who the slimmer version of yourself needs to be. 
Peace.

author: @adamdietrich4677
text:
I was a fat kid. In 7th grade I weighed 180 pounds. I remember times where I would sit on the couch with 4 Oreos, finish them, then go back to the cupboard to grab four more. I ate whole sleeves of Ritz crackers, and loved demolishing bags of Twizzlers. I did all of this before, during, and after I would sit inside and play Halo 3 or Minecraft on my 360.

 Puberty and after school sports helped me stretch out and loose about 30 pounds, but here I am today, at 19 years old looking skinny with a shirt on but uncomfortable taking off my shirt off at a pool. A lot of people call this body type "skinny fat." I tried running. During the first few months in the summer of quarantine I ran 2 miles every other morning and pushed my mile time to 5:50 at its best. Afterwards I would refuel by eating a breakfast of a turkey cheese bagel sandwich and a protein shake. After this meal I always ate a standard lunch and dinner. I didn't see any results in the two months that I did this so I eventually gave up. My stamina was really increasing, but my body hadn't changed.

I went off to college and ran on occasion but ended up making a bad habit eating unhealthy foods, not getting enough sleep, and consuming alcohol. I felt pretty hopeless. I hated the way my chest and abs were rounded by remnants of fat I had from childhood as a result of all those Oreos, and how I had just been adding onto the fire at this point.


I wish I could say I've made it, or that I'm the person who reached his goal and is living in his dream body. The reality is that I'm not there yet. I have a long way to go. Looking back, I now understand why my running stint didn't do anything for my physique. The amount of calories I ate to "refuel" after my runs, and the lunch and dinner I ate after that was undoing the work I had been putting in. A single bagel is anywhere from 250-400 calories. This doesn't even include the meat, cheese, and protein shake I would consume. A 2 mile run will only burn around 300 calories. At my current weight of 150 lbs, my allowance calories for maintenance is about 1500-1750 calories. With a roughly 900 calorie "refuel" meal and the 2 meals I would eat after, I always ended up over my allowance without even knowing it. This realization is why I've recently started a new journey to finally get rid of those Oreos strapped to my chest and belly. 

Extreme Intermittent fasting and being in a caloric deficit has a lot of fans and haters. I am both. I hate being hungry, but I now also understand the logic behind it, and how to reduce my hunger. I've been doing this for 3 weeks now, and I'm barely starting to see a tad of my fat go away, but its working. There are multiple things I've learned while doing this. One, intermittent fasting is not a free pass to eat whatever you want during the feeding window. Second, Calorie counting is essential. Sometimes getting full off food happens, sometimes it doesn't. Third, hunger is powerful. Anyone who diets knows this, but water can be a best friend for this, because it can help top off meals and keep you from snacking. To do a successful calorie restricted diet, a deficit of 500 calories is ample. For me, my recommended calorie intake to keep my current body weight is 1500 calories, so I eat rough 1000. For me personally, I love eggs, and I'm a big fan of consistency. I've been eating 4 eggs every morning the past 3 weeks, alongside oat bread toast without butter, cucumber, and good carbs like plums and apples, as well as avocado halves for good fats and some hummus here and there. When I add these calories up after my meal, I'm happy when it comes to 900-1100 calories because I know that that deficit is slowly but surely chipping away at my bodies natural source of energy apart from food: fat.

I will admit eating one meal a day is extreme. I'm still not fully used to it and I have cravings for those 200 calorie nature valley bars (they taste like heaven), but nothing feels better than resisting those unhealthy temptations. Living like this has been a sacrifice. When I'm out with my friends I'll have to sit in a car smelling like Canes sauce, Texas toast, and chicken, knowing I can't partake in God's great blessing to earth Raising Canes. 

I'm not sure if anyone's gonna read this. It's an old video after all, but If you do, I just want to let you know that sticking to something even when its  hard is infinitely valuable. Sometimes the support from those around you while you are doing the thing you've set your mind to is nonexistent. I've had multiple people say that I'm doing it all wrong and that I should stop, all while they cram their faces with whatever they want. However, I know that I've lived in my body with its crappy metabolism and leftover chub for too long to give in and live like the people who have God-tier metabolisms and eat whatever they want. Like this lady said in her TED talk, Imagine the healthy looking and feeling person you want to be and win small battles every day until one day, you'll look in the mirror and hardly recognize yourself. That's the day that the support and praise from all the people who told you to stop will come, and by then, you won't need it because its you who got you there. 

Once this is over and I've reached my goal of shedding those pounds, I plan on lifting, eating a caloric surplus, and getting bigger. I'm thinking once I reach my first goal I'll come back here to reread what I've wrote and see what progress I've made. Thanks for reading.

EDIT: Changing my strategy to eat more calories and work out more so I can gain muscle and weight since I am actually teetering on being underweight now.

SECOND EDIT: wow so I kinda forgot I wrote this, and checked it out only recently to find the original post had over 100 likes and multiple comments. My thoughts on everything I wrote about here have certainly changed a bit over the course of the year since posting because of my own personal experiences since then. For me as a young 20 year old man, hunger is something I can really struggle with. I look back on the time period where I was only eating one meal a day consisting of 4 eggs and toast as a dark time. I did a lot of research online around that time an apparently there are numerous health benefits for OMAD, but what works for some doesn't necessarily work for all. I lost a lot of weight, but my body didn't discriminate between fat and muscle while shedding pounds. I ended up looking less full and more frail. This wasn't the body I wanted. 

Friends of mine convinced to have a change of heart and to take a different approach to getting a body I was proud of. Going to the gym has altered the way I view food and my own body. I started small at Planet fitness and quickly realized that if I was going to be working hard in the gym, I needed to properly fuel myself with ample amounts of good healthy food. Especially as a young man, my body reacted positively to the new regimen. I was getting classic noob gains of muscle. The problem of looking a little fat around the midsection has come back, but mentally, having muscle helps everything look proportional. Not only do I look a lot better but I feel better too. I've decided to delay my gratification by accepting a bulk cut strategy for the long term as well. 

I think one of the main things I've learned through this whole process is that trying something is better than trying nothing. No one who's an expert at anything ever would have gotten that way if they didn't risk failure by at least attempting whatever it was. For me that was doing something as severe as eating one meal a day to discover that I needed a different approach to reaching my goals. So if you're on the fence about what your next move should be, I'd honestly just say "try something" and stick with it. Evaluate and assess where you are, learn patience, and then figure out if your strategy needs to be adjusted.

author: @Artsy-333
text:
I wrote a lot about my recent experience, so if you have time then do read my long ass comment. 

I was insecure of my moustache, as a teen, I'm not at the exact age off shaving facial hair off and it just feels extremely uncomfortable to ask my parents about it. Also I feel that every time I cut it, shave it whatever it just grows back even more. I did feel it wasn't a good feature but it became an insecurity when my cousin brothers teased me about it. I felt embarrassed also because the cousin who had said that was conventionally quite attractive. Hearing you ugly from an attractive person sucks even more. Then after months of months of being insecure, a friend told me, that I may have more upper lip hair and a noticable moustache but I rock it. I look pretty with it. I realised that just because I'm a little hairy doesn't mean I'm not pretty. It is common for adolescents to have hair and there are many girls like me, infact some have hair even more than me. I'm so pretty that even the body hair or acne can't  hide how much of a fine shit I am. When I don't mind body hair,acne,chubby body, crooked teeth, color, etc. on somebody, then why should anyone else? And if they do they're just piece of little shits. And again when brother cousins came for the holidays, that same cousin said that I potentially have more hair growing on my upper lip than my other brother, I replied with a nonchalant tone, that did you not study basic biology in 8th grade? Hair is natural. Their reactions took a hit. They were like 8th grade was so long ago, I don't remember, blah blah. When you have the confidence when someone points your insecurity and you show that it's not a weakness that person understands that this  person will not be embarrassed/humiliated/bothered by no matter what I say, they quit. You have to make that defense wall.

author: @KatieCottingham
text: I'm glad you got more comfortable in your body. Please though, don't get into the habit of sitting with your legs crossed, and this goes for EVERYONE. The progressive damage done to your legs vascular condition is not something you necessarily notice immediately, but it's an unnecessary risk especially for women and doubly for women on birth control because it increases the risk of a DVT that can be thrown to your heart, lungs, or brain. In my A&P 1 lecture, I was lucky and got a freshly retired oncologist who had just left practice after running one of the most prestigious departments in the US. She brought in additional examples of photos and documentation from earlier in her practice of the women they couldn't save. Because their unnecessary deaths shouldn't be forgotten. That stuck with me. Years later I looked into it further. I stopped crossing my legs at all. My calves have thanked me in more ways than one going into my 30s.

I'd like to be about 10lbs lighter. But I do a lot of outdoor work from homesteading and I feel like I've got the best muscle tone in my life!  I will just flex and pose in the mirror for so long because for the first time in 4 years I feel like my body is the way it's supposed to be.  The little things like walking/running across the yard or lifting a heavy thing have become so much easier.  It was a truly humbling experience and I'm grateful to be on the other side.  Prayers and good energy to anyone struggling to find a body they're happy in❤

author: @kcpugh5601
text:
So true! I'm 5'9 and I went from 160 in high school to 210 over the epidemic to 155, and now I'm around a healthy 170 with muscle. Some of the things I noticed are:
1. My cold tolerance is shot. I used to be able to walk around with minimal layers during the winter, but now I need to insulate like nobody's business. I used to think people who wore hoodies in 70 degree weather were ridiculous, but now I always bring one just in case.
2. Certain exercises are a lot easier, but some are actually more uncomfortable. I lost padding around my hip bones, so now exercises like weighted back extensions suck. But hey, stairs don't make me wheeze anymore.
3. Your features look sharper. I kinda miss my chubby cheeks, but I do like how my cheekbones are more defined now.
4. Yes, more access to cute clothes, but not being able to wear your old clothes you got attached to sucks.
5. On the clothes thing, not being sure if you want to keep your bigger clothes 'just in case'. I also got rid of some of my cute clothes after I gained weight because I thought I wasn't going to lose it anytime soon, only to regret it later.
6. Realizing how mean I was to myself when I was chubby. She deserved just as much love and affection as I do currently.
7. Getting really uncomfortable when your friends make comments about their bodies or yours. I have friends who only knew me after I lost weight, and they constantly call me scrawny or say I lack curves(I don't).
8. Feeling weird about how much or how little I eat. Thank God I didn't have any family making comments on it, but with my more active lifestyle, I tend to eat more. Sometimes I have to remind myself that it's okay to eat when I'm hungry because I have leftover feelings I need to be "doing more" to "earn it."
9. Realizing how toxic the body positivity movement can be. A lot of the times it's more about encouraging bad behavior rather than learning to love yourself at any size. You can be okay with how you look and still want to make healthier choices.
10. I still do the shirt tug thing.
Anyways, good luck to anyone on a weight loss, weight gain, or weight maintaining journey. Prioritize your health over looks and remember that you deserve to be loved at any size.

author: @TheFuzzyFixer
text:
Not to overshadow what Sophie is sharing here, rather to build off of it-the other things no one tells you about losing weight (from the male perspective of losing >100 lbs) are:
1) the loose skin thing. Fortunately that goes away in most places after a few months, but around the pecs and belly area, that takes a yr or more. Working out regularly does help and fill the area with some muscle, which does kinda help blend that in a little-though it can be very stubborn. Just keep at it folks and just go with the mindset that it's not "ugly" it's a badge of courage and medal of victory. Easier said than done, but you would be amazed how many people are actually super supportive and not judgemental if you rock it with that kind of mindset. 

2) having to get a whole new wardrobe. Probably the ladies in your audience are like "Heck yeah!", but as a guy: I hate shopping and I already found the clothes I liked in the first place-they just now don't fit at all. Although, I have been really getting into the western/cowboy/country aesthetic over the last year , so that's actually been really enjoyable to shop for. I would just caution anyone on their weight loss journey to wait until they've stabilized before totally exchanging their whole wardrobe. Just get a few pieces at a time. You'll find that the weight will fluctuate quite a bit once you're close to your target, especially if you're doing it natural (like diet/exercise), but it will stabilize about a year in once you maintain target weight. 

3) counseling/therapy. I've mentioned before, but I'm a male that suffered through an eating disorder-still of course dealing with it, but much better off now-where I'd binge until I balloon up like 50-100lbs (300+ in total), then starve myself until I'm like down to the 160's/170's. Rinse and repeat. For reference, I'm 6'1" and a broader frame, so I look perfect around 195-210lbs (which is still super thin for me, like waist size 34-which was my early highschool pants size), so dropping as low as I have, I looked literally skeletal. But, like most ED's I used food as both comfort and punishment-so no longer having that crutch I had really no other choice but to seek therapy, which was initially terrifying. I'm also from a culture where mental health is just not a thing or considered valid in any way. But at that point I need to deal with the underlying issues of depression, anxiety, PTSD, and the effects of TBI. Now of course I'm grateful I have done so as things like rapid eye movement therapy and CBT have literally changed my life for the better. Now at almost 40 I'm finally living life for the first time. My only regret is not doing it sooner, could have had at least 10 more years of enjoying life, but better late than never. So, if you use food as part of your coping, whether positively or negatively (i.e. comfort or punishment), just be prepared to seek therapy as part of your weight loss journey-you'll be grateful you did. And frankly, it's paramount to your long term success. You've got to get mind, body, and soul aligned to really be living your best life. 

4) how long it really takes and the rollercoaster ride that it is. There's a lot of putting in huge amounts of work, getting that initial drop and then nothing for a while -or even tracking backwards. And of course the relapses, especially if you're dealing with weight issues from the ED end of things. This is completely normal. You're not failing. Always remember it's a journey, not a destination. And it takes time with trial and error sometimes. You're changing how your body works, how your mind works, battling those "demons" underlying everything, and changing your entire relationship with food.  Those are a lot of moving parts and each one needs to be addressed, which takes time and a lot of effort. You're essentially breaking yourself down to the core and rebuilding yourself. This takes time. There will be relapses when it gets too hard or when you uncover something very deeply traumatic. Give yourself that little bit of permission to take a breather when you need to. What you want isn't the quick fix, you want to entirely change the course of the rest of your life and health-physical mental-for the better. Those times of feeling like it's too much, or you can't take it anymore, or it's impossible-these are all normal. These are signs you're on the right track, not failing. Allow yourself to feel and process that whole range of emotions from start to finish. Stuffing it all down is what caused this in the first place, so don't go back to it. Trust me, everyone on this journey goes through these same barriers and hurdles. You're not weird or the only one, even if they don't talk about it or share on social media (not saying Sophie is doing that, just in general). You will get through it if you allow yourself too. They say it takes at least 4 weeks to really get into a new habit and up to 12 weeks to really be able to maintain it. 

5) not worrying about the numbers on the scale. Yup, that's right. Weight loss isn't about the numbers on the scale. In fact, you'll be better off not even looking at a scale. What's now considered the most valid clinic sign of a good weight isn't the absolute number or even the BMI any longer-it's actually the hip to waist ratio. Newer studies have found the hip to waist ratio (you're hip to waist ratio specifically, not relative to someone one else), is the better marker to consequences if inappropriate weight. Things like metabolic syndrome, hormone balance, etc. And even the aesthetic of how you look. 

6) stop focusing on other people's aesthetic or absolute weight (the numbers on the scale). You can have 2 people of the same height weigh entirely differently and yet not look like there's any difference. Things like bone density, muscle density, overall frame and build all effect the absolute weight. Just because you, per the scale numbers, might be "heavy" or "light" means actually nothing. As long as you feel strong, healthy, confident, and sexy-you're where you need to be. 

7) different frames need a different target goal. People come in all shapes and sizes. Targeting a "standardized" weight on the scale can actually lead you down the wrong path. It's ok if you're a taller person, a shorter person, one with broader shoulders or hips, narrow and thin, one with a big butt, or one with no butt (✋, I've got the whole Hank Hill thing going on. Comment if you know that reference). This is where your specific hip to waist ratio becomes a better metric to measure yourself by if you're into that sort of thing. Myself, I'm a tallish (6'1") board shoulders and kind of board hips for a dude. In the 170's lbs I look skeletal, but at 210 I look and feel just right. The next guy can be 6'3", but be of a narrower thinner frame and looks/feels perfect in the 170's, but would look "fat" in the 200's. So go with what feels/looks right for your specific frame. This will take some trial and error, just give yourself the permission to experiment and find where you feel right. 

8) of course there are great things about losing weight. Like not getting out of breath and dizzy from just putting your shoes on. Feeling agile and mobile. Not being type 2 diabetic any longer (of course I still need to be careful with sugar intake). Not having dangerously high blood pressure. Not being too fatigued to do anything all day (both when super heavy and when way too underweight). Feeling confident, strong, and powerful-not just from the way your body feels, but from also getting your mind and soul in a better way. Plus you've vanquished a foe that has been controlling your life for far too long and that is a huge booster. 

Anyway, I hope this can also further help anyone reading this in your weight loss journey as well. Good luck, but really you don't need luck-you got this!

author: @lisbethraun5320
text:
I must say, the claim of losing 20 pounds in a month strikes me as rather concerning, particularly as it's not specifying its target audience. Such aggressive weight loss targets would be downright dangerous for someone who's underweight or at a healthy weight.

Whilst it's technically possible for someone who is significantly overweight, obese, or morbidly obese to lose 20 pounds in a month, particularly at the beginning of their weight loss journey, it's worth unpacking what this weight loss actually comprises:

- Initially, a good portion (potentially 5-8 pounds) would likely be water weight, particularly if reducing carbohydrate intake
- Some would unfortunately be lean muscle mass (potentially 2-4 pounds)
- The remainder could be fat loss, though this varies dramatically based on starting weight, metabolic rate, and activity levels

The NHS and British medical guidelines typically recommend a safe and sustainable weight loss of 1-2 pounds per week, which amounts to roughly 4-8 pounds per month. Even for those carrying significant excess weight, anything more dramatic than that tends to be difficult to maintain long-term and may lead to the dreaded 'yo-yo' effect.

Moreover, without proper medical supervision, such rapid weight loss could lead to rather nasty consequences: nutritional deficiencies, gallstones, and metabolic disruptions, to name but a few. It's worth noting that any 'one-size-fits-all' approach to such significant weight loss is, frankly, quite irresponsible.

The sensible approach would be to consult one's GP or a registered dietitian for personalised advice based on individual circumstances, medical history, and current health status.

moreover, without proper medical supervision, such rapid weight loss could lead to rather nasty consequences: nutritional deficiencies, gallstones, and metabolic disruptions, to name but a few. it's worth noting that any 'one-size-fits-all' approach to such significant weight loss is, frankly, quite irresponsible.

the sensible approach would be to consult one's gp or a registered dietitian for personalised advice based on individual circumstances, medical history, and current health status.

- Average 8 hours of sleep
- Protein (1-1.2g per pound of Lean Body Mass)
- Heavy Lifting for muscle mass & strength
- Cardio to burn extra calories + heart health
- Ate high fiber foods. Helped keep me feeling fuller for longer

This is a very broad example, so many factors can be at play, you can go get a metabolic test to see your personalized calorie maintenance. And  of course cardio, gym, etc burn even more calories. But hope this gives someone a starting point as it did me.
